extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and responding to double patenting rejections, terminal disclaimer requirements, and the interplay of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 and 103(c) (CREATE Act) in prosecution and reexamination. Focused on when and how examiners should apply rejections and require statements/disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirements (37 CFR 1.321)
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or a patent to be granted that is used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent. The requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample forms of a terminal disclaimer, and guidance as to the filing and treatment of a terminal disclaimer, are provided in MPEP § 1490. A terminal disclaimer may be used to overcome double patenting rejections by disclaiming the terminal portion of the later patent's term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer enforceability provision (37 CFR 1.321(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) requires that a terminal disclaimer 'include a provision that any patent granted on that application or any patent subject to the reexamination proceeding shall be enforceable only for and during such period that said patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must ensure the terminal disclaimer filed to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection based on commonly owned conflicting claims includes this enforceability provision. Failure to include it can defeat the disclaimer's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirements for joint research agreements (37 CFR 1.321(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth the requirements for a terminal disclaimer where the claimed invention resulted from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventions arise from a joint research agreement, filing a terminal disclaimer that includes each one of the conflicting double patenting references is also necessary to avoid ownership problems between parties to a joint research agreement. Use 1.321(d) requirements to craft disclaimers for such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer required to overcome nonstatutory double patenting for applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required in an application to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995 and claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) of the filing date of the patent or application which forms the basis for the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) sets 20-year patent terms from filing and 154(b) allows for term adjustments, a terminal disclaimer is still necessary to avoid the potential for multiple patents with different expiration dates and harassment of accused infringers. Examiners should cite this MPEP section or the Official Gazette notice when applicants argue a disclaimer is unnecessary due to the change to 35 U.S.C. 154.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership exclusion (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1)-(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person, which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102, shall not preclude patentability where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For purposes of this subsection, subject matter developed by another person and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person if: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute shields patentability from certain prior art only when these ownership/agreements conditions are met. Examiners should apply the statutory tests (including the definition of 'joint research agreement') when determining whether a reference is disqualified under 103(c). See MPEP § 706.02(l) for detailed definition of common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'joint research agreement' (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of paragraph (2), the term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agreement must be written and cover experimental/developmental/research work in the claimed invention's field. Examiners must verify that the agreement meets this statutory definition when applying 103(c)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualifying a commonly owned patent/published application as prior art (37 CFR 1.130(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 on a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication which is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), and the inventions are not identical but not patentably distinct, and the inventions are owned by the same party, the applicant or owner may disqualify the patent or patent application publication as prior art by submission of: (1) A terminal disclaimer in accordance with § 1.321(c); and (2) An oath or declaration stating that the application or patent under reexamination and patent or published application are currently owned by the same party, and that the inventor named in the application or patent under reexamination is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should accept this combination (terminal disclaimer + oath/declaration) to disqualify the reference as prior art where the statutory conditions are met. See MPEP for form and procedural handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: When double patenting rejections apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. Claims may also be rejected on grounds of nonstatutory double patenting in certain non-commonly owned applications that claim inventions resulting from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement (CREATE Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double patenting where claims are not patentably distinct and would improperly extend patent term or allow multiple patents covering the same invention. Cite case law (e.g., In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) when appropriate. Use terminal disclaimers or statutory exclusions as applicable to resolve issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATE Act treatment for non-commonly owned inventions (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to the CREATE Act, non-commonly owned applications or patents that are subject to a joint research agreement may be treated as if they are 'commonly owned' for determining obviousness if conditions are met. Two inventions come within 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (D) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should apply these four conditions for applications pending on or after December 10, 2004 (and certain reexaminations) to determine whether a reference is disqualified under 103(c). See MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) and CREATE Act legislative history for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and sequencing of double patenting and 102/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should make both a double patenting rejection based on common ownership and a rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 prior art when the facts support both rejections. Until applicant has established that a reference is disqualified as prior art under the joint research agreement exclusion of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner should NOT apply a double patenting rejection based on a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prematurely apply double patenting based on a joint research agreement until the applicant has borne out the statutory disqualification. Consult MPEP § 706.07(a) and § 804 regarding making such Office actions final when new subsequent double patenting rejections arise from disqualified references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority determination when 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) applies
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of priority is not required when two inventions are commonly owned as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per 37 CFR 1.78(c), examiners may require assignee statements about common ownership; if assignee states 103(c) applies, no further inquiry is needed as to prior inventor. If assignee states 103(c) does not apply, the assignee must indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor; failure to comply may result in abandonment. Use form paragraphs 8.27, 8.28, 8.28.01 to require naming the prior inventor where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.78(c) examiner inquiries and assignee obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application or a patent under reexamination and at least one other application naming different inventors are owned by the same person and contain conflicting claims, and there is no statement of record indicating common ownership at the time the later invention was made, the Office may require the assignee to state whether the claimed inventions were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the later invention was made, and if not, indicate which named inventor is the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs 8.27, 8.28 and 8.28.01 may be used to require the applicant to identify the prior inventor under 37 CFR 1.78(c). The assignee must respond to avoid abandonment. Before making such a requirement (which can lead to abandonment), the examiner must ensure conflicting claims exist as defined in MPEP § 804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 not obviated solely by terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 cannot be obviated solely by filing a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers address extension-of-term concerns (nonstatutory double patenting) but do not remove substantive prior art rejections under 102 or 103. Examiners must still make or maintain appropriate prior art rejections where supported by the record. See specific instructions about provisional rejections and form paragraphs when copending references are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provisional rejection form paragraphs (7.21.01, 7.15.01) for copending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.21.01 is used to provisionally reject under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over a copending application which has a common assignee or at least one common inventor. Form paragraph 7.15.01 is used to provisionally reject under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by a copending application which has a common assignee or at least one common inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisional rejections are based on the presumption that the copending application will be published or patented. They may be overcome by showings under 37 CFR 1.132 or 1.131 (derivation or earlier date of invention) or by showing the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Do not use these provisional paragraphs where the copending application is disqualified under 103(c) for applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004. Apply AIPA rules to determine 102(e) dates as noted in the Examiner Notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph guidance for requiring prior-inventor statements (¶ 8.27, ¶ 8.28, ¶ 8.28.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 8.27 and ¶ 8.28 are form paragraphs to require naming the prior inventor or to assert that claims are not patentably distinct; ¶ 8.28.01 provides advisory information relating to ¶ 8.28. They explain when refusal to institute an interference occurs and when identifying the prior inventor is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ¶ 8.27 when claims are for the same invention and priority under 102(g)/(f) must be resolved; use ¶ 8.28 when claims are not patentably distinct but there is no evidence of common ownership at time of invention. ¶ 8.28.01 should follow ¶ 8.28 and be used only once in an Office action. If the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) apply, obviousness rejections may be obviated; if not, make appropriate double patenting and prior art rejections.
